title: Guided visits — one session each — to what the other doors' Camp 1 taught, tagged and unblended: the light in me sees the light in you
hook: the last visit: your very first word, and how other houses say something near it in their own words
tomorrow: the first mountain, from the top

segments.voice: The strand's name for the week, rosarium, has held six visits. Yesterday's was the rosary: beads in the hand, a story in the heart. Did your fingers keep a quiet count? Day three hundred twenty-nine.

Last visit of the week, and it starts at home. Day one of this whole path, three hundred twenty-eight days ago, your first word was namaste. Palms together, a small bow. And your very first carry: the light in me sees the light in you. You've carried it for most of a year. This week you've been a guest in six other houses. It turns out the idea underneath that line lives, in different clothes, in other houses too. Today, the last guided visit: what that line sounds like when other people say it, in their own words.
screen: `DAY ONE: NAMASTE.` → `YOUR FIRST LINE: THE LIGHT IN YOU.` → `OTHER HOUSES, THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Start at your own door. Namaste is namah, a bow, plus te, to you. I bow to you. That's what the syllables say. The light-in-me line is what the bow means: many Hindus say you bow to the divine in the other person, the same atman you met on day ten. The words are the bow; the line is the reason for it. Now the neighbors, one at a time, each in their own words. The Jewish house begins on the Bible's first page. In the 1917 translation: "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him." Every human face, Jews say, carries that image. One rabbi in the midrash warns that whoever puts another person to shame should remember whose likeness they are shaming. The Sikh house has a hymn sung every evening in many gurdwaras, the Aarti of Guru Nanak, which says, in effect, that one Light is in everyone, and that Light is God's. The Quakers, a Christian community, have a phrase from their founder George Fox in the 1600s: to answer that of God in everyone. Quakers still use it to explain why they don't bow to titles, and why they sit in silence together. These aren't one teaching wearing four costumes. A Jew, a Sikh, a Quaker and a Hindu would each explain their line differently, and each would want to be heard in their own words. That was this week's whole rule. But from your door, you can notice something: in many houses, people have looked at the person in front of them and seen more than a person. Seva, the breath, dhikr, Shabbat, grace, the rosary. Six houses, and now one bow.
screen: `NAMASTE: I BOW TO YOU.` · `IN THE IMAGE OF GOD.` · `ONE LIGHT IN EVERYONE.` · `THAT OF GOD IN EVERYONE.` · then, large: `THE ONE HOUSE, SEEN FROM YOUR DOOR.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the faces from this week's visits: the woman ladling dal, the teacher saying just know it, the Sufi circle, the family lighting candles, the choir, the grandmother with beads. Don't blend them. Let each one be itself. Then, if you like, bring your palms together and give each a small bow in your mind, one at a time. Then one more, for the next person you'll see today. The bell holds the time.
Namaste, I bow to you. The strand's name for the whole week of visits comes home: namaste, and the light other houses see in a face.

segments.voice: Your line: more than a person. Today, look at one person the way this week's houses taught. Day three hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: Hindus greet each other with palms together and namaste or namaskar, and many explain the bow as honoring the divine in the other; Jews, Sikhs and Quakers each have their own teachings about God's image or light in every person.

fork.setup: a friend asks what the syllables of namaste actually say. you've walked this path for 329 days. what do you tell them?
options: the light in me sees the light in you, word for word.
I bow to you; the light line is why many bow.
it's just a way of saying goodbye.
fork.reveal: namah, a bow, plus te, to you. many Hindus say the bow honors the divine in the other, which is where the light line comes from.

original.note: Sanskrit namaḥ, a bow, + te, to you: I bow to you.

trapdoor: what you thought: namaste is just hello.
what it means: I bow to you, and many Hindus say the bow is to the divine in the other: the light in me sees the light in you.
what a scholar hears: te is a dative 'to you', so the grammar itself makes the greeting a small offering, not a statement.

notes: Week-end look-back for week 47. Genesis 1:27 quoted from JPS 1917; verify.
The rabbinic line about shaming someone as shaming the image is paraphrased and now attributed to Genesis Rabbah 24:7 (Rabbi Tanhuma); a Jewish reviewer should confirm the paraphrase.
Aarti at Ang 663 (Dhanasri, 'sabh mahi jot jot hai soi') paraphrased; confirm it is sung in the evening in many gurdwaras (as part of Sohila/Aarti practice).
George Fox's phrase ('answering that of God in every one', 1656) is paraphrased without quotation marks; the link to Quaker refusal of hat-honor and silent worship is a common explanation.
Namaste framing follows the day 1 manuscript: namas, I bow; te, to you; 'the light in me sees the light in you' as what the bow means. Keeper to confirm.
Index word/carry repeated for the week; see day 323 notes.

Audit (2026-09-30, 10% sample): the line 'the rabbis taught that to shame someone is to shame it' was cited to Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, which doesn't say that; now attributed to one rabbi (Rabbi Tanhuma) in Genesis Rabbah 24:7, paraphrased, and the source entry changed to match.
